row.note: Genesis forms the human from ground and then gives life by divine breath. It provides a close biblical sequence for the commentary's ordered body and its cited Q 32:9 breath, while retaining an earthly material origin.

Job says God's hands fashioned him all around, then protests that the same maker turns to destroy him. The shared embodied formation is set in a lament, a deliberate tension with the praise of creating and proportioning in Q 87:2.
Job figures his prenatal making as liquid poured like milk and curdled like cheese. That material, staged image belongs beside the commentary's formed and unformed embryonic body.

Job describes being clothed with skin and flesh and woven with bones and sinews. It is a concrete bodily counterpart to the commentary's claim that creation and setting right can be heard as bodily formation.

After the anatomical images, Job says God granted life and guarded his spirit. It joins formed flesh to a divinely sustained life, as the commentary joins proportioning to breath and eventual revivification.
Job says a person's days and months are determined and bounded by God. This directly supplies the temporal side of the commentary's particular measure (qaddara) across a human life.
Job grounds equal human standing in one maker who made both people in the womb and fashioned them there. The shared point is divine womb-formation, not merely a general creator title.
The psalmist places dependence on God from the mother's belly onward. Together with its old-age plea, it gives the lifespan arc that the commentary hears in child-rearing and senescence.
The same speaker asks not to be abandoned in old age when strength fails. This is a specific biblical counterpart to the commentary's move from fetal formation through maturity toward old age.

The psalm explicitly compares a human's days to grass and a flowering field. It closely matches the commentary's pairing of the ordered body with the pasture that dries up as one warning about mortal life.
The following verse makes the grass vanish when the wind passes over it. It supplies the disappearance that gives the body-and-pasture comparison its warning force.
When God takes away breath, living creatures die and return to dust. This links breath, bodily mortality, and earth in the same sequence the commentary connects to creation and resurrection.

God sends breath, creatures are created, and the ground is renewed. The verse places animate creation and revived earth together, paralleling the commentary's juxtaposition of body and watered pasture.
The psalm attributes the inward parts and covering in the mother's womb to God. It is a direct counterpart to the commentary's womb enclosure and fetal bodily formation.
The speaker's frame is made in secret and woven in hidden depths. Its hidden craftsmanship gives a biblical form to the commentary's transition from unformed to fully shaped body.

God sees the speaker's unformed substance, and the days are written before they arrive. The verse combines embryo imagery with a measured lifespan, the two strands of the commentary's reading of created and apportioned life.

Ecclesiastes invokes the formation of bones in a pregnant woman as something humans do not know, then extends that ignorance to God's work. It checks any attempt to turn the commentary's lexical fetal images into a claimed account of fetal mechanics.

row.basis: earth gives birth to the dead
row.note: Isaiah calls sleepers in dust to awake and portrays earth as giving birth to the dead. The birth image makes an especially close counterpart to the commentary's inference from prenatal formation to resurrection.
Isaiah names the Lord as both maker and one who forms the addressee from the womb. This directly joins the two creation verbs that the commentary develops as fetal formation.

The speaker again identifies himself as maker of all and former of the addressee from the womb. Its cosmic and prenatal scopes together illuminate the commentary's claim that a measured human body belongs to a larger created order.
God addresses those carried from the belly and borne from the womb. It begins a divine care sequence at prenatal and birth stages, matching the commentary's life-course reading.

row.basis: until old age and gray hair
row.note: The same divine bearer remains present until old age and gray hair. This is a particularly exact lifespan counterpart to the commentary's movement from the womb through maturity to senescence.
The servant says the Lord formed him from the womb for service. It joins bodily formation to calling, a useful counterpart both to Q 87:2's formation and to the recited commission in Q 87:6.

row.basis: formed, known, and appointed before birth
row.note: Jeremiah is known before womb-formation and appointed before emergence. The verse makes divine formation part of a life directed toward a purpose, sharpening the commentary's measure-and-guidance claim.

In Ezekiel's vision God promises breath to dry bones so that they will live. It supplies an explicit bodily-revival analogue for the commentary's citation of embryonic creation as evidence for raising the dead.

God orders sinews, flesh, skin, and breath onto bones. The ordered rebuilding of a body is a close counterpart to formed flesh, bodily proportion, and later life; Ezekiel's own vision then identifies this with Israel's restoration.

row.basis: breath gives life to assembled bodies
row.note: Once breath enters, the assembled bodies live and stand. The verse completes the formation-to-life sequence that the commentary traces from fetal body to resurrection.
God promises to put his spirit within the people so that they live. Its own national-restoration setting makes the bodily image an interpretive rather than a simple individual-resurrection equation.
Daniel depicts many sleeping in earth's dust awakening to divergent lasting destinies. It gives the eschatological endpoint of the commentary's earth-to-body-to-resurrection arc.
Isaiah's voice calls all flesh grass and human constancy a field flower. The explicit flesh-and-grass equation strongly parallels the commentary's body and drying pasture as two faces of one warning.
Grass withers and the flower fades when the Lord's breath blows on it. It adds the agency of divine breath to the commentary's life-and-pasture contrast.

row.basis: molded into flesh in mother's womb
row.note: Wisdom's speaker says he was molded into flesh in a mother's womb. It is a late Jewish, explicitly prenatal formulation of the bodily shaping developed in the commentary.
The next verse describes gestation in a fixed period and bodily material from seed and blood. Its timed, material account closely meets the commentary's womb gathering and measured formation.
The speaker moves from womb formation to birth and breathing the common air. That transition is useful beside the commentary's formed body followed by divine breath and life.

Wisdom says God arranged all things by measure, number, and weight. This is an unusually exact Jewish formulation of the commentary's account of qaddara as placing each thing in a particular measure and form.

row.basis: from mother's womb to return to earth
row.note: Sirach frames the human burden from leaving the mother's womb until returning to the mother of all. It explicitly spans the bodily life course from birth to death that the commentary assembles from its roots.

The mother of the martyrs says she does not know how her children came to be in her womb and denies that she gave them life or set their elements in order. It closely mirrors the commentary's created, ordered fetus while locating agency in the Creator.

The mother says the Creator will return life and breath to her sons. The verse directly makes prenatal formation an argument for resurrection, exactly the inferential move foregrounded by the commentary.
The mother points to heaven, earth, and the human race as made by God. In her martyrdom context this supports hope beyond death, extending the commentary's creation-to-resurrection reasoning.

row.basis: formed in wisdom; openings and cavities
row.note: The Asher Yatzar blessing praises the one who formed the human in wisdom with openings and cavities whose proper functioning sustains life. It offers a Jewish liturgical analogue to the commentary's well-proportioned, disease-free body ordered by wisdom.

row.basis: parents' material and God's life-giving share
row.note: The Talmud distinguishes parental contributions to bones, flesh, and other features from God's gift of spirit, soul, senses, and understanding. It is a detailed Jewish account of an ordered body joined to life and capacity.

row.basis: fetus in womb taught Torah then made to forget
row.note: Niddah says the fetus is taught Torah in the womb and an angel causes it to forget at birth. The combination of womb, instruction, and forgetting is a specific meeting with Q 87:6's recitation and not-forgetting beside the commentary's womb sense for its root.

row.basis: grain buried and clothed in rising
row.note: Rabbi Meir answers a resurrection question with wheat that is buried bare and emerges clothed. The rabbinic analogy joins vegetal renewal to bodily resurrection, like the commentary's body-and-pasture pairing.
Paul says God gives all people life, breath, and everything. It is a concise New Testament counterpart to the commentary's sequence from shaped body to enlivening breath.

Paul says God determined allotted times and the bounds of peoples' habitation. This gives a concrete New Testament use of divine determination as ordered measure, rather than an imported lexical equation.

row.basis: Spirit gives life to mortal bodies
row.note: The Spirit who raised Jesus will give life to mortal bodies. It directly joins divine indwelling spirit, bodily mortality, and resurrection in the way the commentary connects formation, breath, and revivification.
Paul explicitly asks how the dead are raised and with what sort of body they come. This names the bodily-resurrection question that the commentary raises through Q 75:40.
Paul's seed image says death precedes new life. It provides a vegetal pattern for the commentary's move from a dying pasture and mortal body toward life beyond death.

row.basis: bare grain and body to come
row.note: The sower does not sow the body that will come, but a bare grain. This distinguishes initial material from its later formed body, a strong analogue to the commentary's unformed and completed stages.

row.basis: God gives each seed its body
row.note: God gives the seed a body as he chooses, to each seed its own body. The sentence makes divine assignment of bodily form an explicit resurrection counterpart to creating and proportioning.
Paul contrasts a perishable sown body with an imperishable raised one. It makes the commentary's mortality-and-afterlife warning bodily and eschatological.
The body is sown in weakness and raised in power. This supplies an eschatological reversal of the frailty and declining strength that the commentary associates with old age.
Paul distinguishes a natural body from a raised spiritual body, without discarding bodiliness. It is a useful Christian development of the commentary's body-plus-breath sequence.
Christ will transform the body of lowliness to conform to his glorious body. The verse gives a specifically Christian answer to the commentary's movement from mortal formed body to life after death.

row.basis: rich person and fading grass flower
row.note: James tells the rich to boast in lowliness because they pass away like a flower of grass. It closely matches the commentary's confident garden owner and the warning conveyed by worldly life and withering pasture.

row.basis: sun scorches grass and beauty perishes
row.note: James completes the image: sun scorches the grass, its flower falls, and the rich fade in their pursuits. This gives the image an ethical warning about transient prosperity, as in the commentary's ruined garden.

First Peter quotes the formula that all flesh is like grass and its glory like a grass flower. It is the New Testament's closest verbal and conceptual counterpart to the commentary's juxtaposition of human body and withering pasture.
The human formed from ground is told to return to dust. It supplies the deathward side of the commentary's earth, body, and resurrection sequence, though it does not itself promise revival.

row.basis: hands made and fashioned; request for understanding
row.note: The psalmist says divine hands made and fashioned him, then asks for understanding of commandments. It brings formed person and divinely directed understanding together, bridging Q 87:2-3's creation and guidance.

row.basis: breath to people and spirit to walkers
row.note: Isaiah's creator gives breath to the people on earth and spirit to those who walk on it. This is a compact creation-and-life formulation alongside the commentary's Q 32:9 comparison.

Sirach describes the Lord assigning created works their portions and arranging them in order. It is a Jewish development of the commentary's claim that each thing is put in a particular measure and mode.

row.basis: human from earth and returned to it
row.note: Sirach says the Lord created humans from earth and lets them return to it. It adds a sapiential version of the soil-to-body-to-death arc underlying the commentary's resurrection reflection.

Onkelos renders the human made living in Genesis as a speaking spirit. That interpretive rendering links the formed and breathed body to speech, which helps place Q 87:6's recitation beside the commentary's bodily reading of its root.

row.basis: origin in a drop; return to dust
row.note: Avot asks a person to remember the bodily origin in a drop and the destination of dust and decay. Its ethical memento turns the life-course images of the commentary into a warning against worldly self-assurance.

Jesus asks which anxious person can add a span to life. This is a focused New Testament counterpart to the commentary's measured human lifespan, with a warning against investing trust in present life.

Jesus describes grass alive today and thrown into an oven tomorrow while arguing for divine care. The image links bodily concern and transient grass, though its immediate point is anxiety rather than resurrection.

John is said to be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb. It makes the womb a site of divine life and vocation, a specific New Testament counterpart to the commentary's prenatal life imagery.
At Mary's greeting, the child leaps in Elizabeth's womb. The narrative gives a concrete fetal bodily response to divine visitation, rather than an abstract use of womb language.

row.basis: growth in wisdom, stature, and favor
row.note: Jesus advances in wisdom, stature, and favor. It is a concise New Testament life-stage counterpart to the commentary's sense of reaching full youth and ordered maturation.

row.basis: life required from the storing rich man
row.note: God tells the rich planner that his life is demanded that night. The sudden end to stored abundance is a close ethical meeting with the commentary's garden owner who trusts worldly security before it vanishes.

Nicodemus hears new birth in literal bodily terms and asks about entering a mother's womb a second time. The question exposes the bodily reading that the following saying redirects, creating a useful contrast with the commentary's literal fetal imagery.

Jesus answers the womb question with birth from water and Spirit. It reworks birth imagery toward eschatological renewal, a Christian counter-reading to place beside the commentary's body-and-breath account.

Paul says God set him apart from his mother's womb and called him through grace. Like Isaiah's womb-formed servant, it joins prenatal life to a directed vocation and the commentary's creation-guidance sequence.

Paul figures the whole creation as groaning together in childbirth. The verse applies labor imagery to creation's movement toward redemption, an interpretive extension of the commentary's body, earth, and resurrection linkage.
Paul contrasts outward decay with inward renewal day by day. It makes the commentary's old-age and enduring-afterlife contrast a present bodily and spiritual discipline.

row.basis: mature person and measure of fullness
row.note: The church's goal is mature adulthood and the measure of Christ's fullness. It takes maturity and measure into an ecclesial-ethical register, rather than describing fetal anatomy.

row.basis: spirit, soul, and body preserved whole
row.note: Paul prays that spirit, soul, and body be kept whole for the Lord's coming. It is a Christian holistic counterpart to the commentary's fully ordered body and its final-life horizon.

First Peter describes a new birth through imperishable seed and enduring word. It offers a Christian extension from bodily birth to lasting life, anticipating the flesh-and-grass contrast in the next verse.

row.basis: Christ's clay healing and primal formation
row.note: Irenaeus reads Jesus' clay healing of the man born blind as the Creator's original art of forming humanity from earth being displayed and restored. This patristic reading makes bodily formation and repair central to resurrection faith.

row.basis: Hebrew qara, calling names after formation
row.note: Hebrew qara, to call or name, belongs to the Semitic q-r-ʾ family also heard in Q 87:6's recitation verb. Here Adam names creatures after their formation, so it supports speech after creation but does not carry the commentary's Arabic womb-closure sense.

Hebrew rabah, to become many, is a cognate family relevant to the commentary's source label r-b-b. Genesis uses it for human fruitfulness and multiplication, not for the Arabic sense of rearing a child stage by stage.

Job calls God kabbir, great or mighty, a cognate family of Arabic kabir. The Hebrew context keeps greatness rather than age in view, which helps distinguish the commentary's age-related Arabic root note from the actual 'great' fire of Q 87:12.

row.basis: from mother's womb to naked return
row.note: Job says he came naked from his mother's womb and will return naked. The saying compresses bodily origin and mortality into the life-course arc that the commentary traces from womb formation to its end.

row.basis: Spirit made me; breath gives life
row.note: Job's interlocutor says God's Spirit made him and the Almighty's breath gives him life. It is a particularly direct Hebrew Bible counterpart to the commentary's formed body followed by enlivening breath.
Elihu imagines God gathering back to himself a creature's spirit and breath. This supplies the withdrawal side of the commentary's body-and-breath sequence.

row.basis: all flesh perishes and returns to dust
row.note: The consequence of withdrawn breath is that all flesh dies and humanity returns to dust. It makes the body, breath, and earth sequence explicit before any resurrection answer is supplied.

row.basis: God knows the frame and remembers dust
row.note: The psalm says God knows the human frame and remembers that humans are dust. It ties bodily construction to earthly frailty, supplementing the commentary's formed body and its eventual decline.

row.basis: dust returns; spirit returns to God
row.note: Ecclesiastes separates the body's return to earth from the spirit's return to God. It gives a sharply stated deathward counterpart to the commentary's body-and-breath account and its afterlife horizon.
Isaiah calls a mortal human being like grass. This directly joins the human body and fading vegetation that the commentary treats as one warning about temporary worldly life.

Wisdom says God created humanity for incorruption and made it in the likeness of divine eternity. It gives a Jewish counterweight to bodily decay that closely matches the commentary's contrast of worldly life with what endures.

row.basis: power over life, death, and return
row.note: Wisdom attributes authority over life and death to God, including bringing people down to Hades and back. It is a direct Jewish formulation of the creation-to-resurrection inference developed in the commentary.

row.basis: dust-made body and breath of life
row.note: Fourth Ezra says God commanded dust to give Adam, a lifeless body formed by divine hands, then breathed life into him. The retelling explicitly combines the commentary's earth, fashioned body, and breath sequence.

row.basis: formed, born, lives, dies, and gives account
row.note: Avot presents human formation, birth, life, death, and judgment as an involuntary ordered sequence. It is a rabbinic whole-life formulation for the stages the commentary assembles from womb to old age and final reckoning.

row.basis: those in tombs hear the voice
row.note: Jesus says all who are in tombs will hear his voice. It supplies a New Testament voice-to-bodily-resurrection counterpart to the commentary's move from divine speech and formation to the raising of the dead.
Those who hear come out, to life or judgment according to their deeds. The bodily emergence and divided final outcome develop the resurrection horizon invoked by the commentary.

row.basis: gives life to dead and calls what is not
row.note: Paul characterizes God as giving life to the dead and calling into being things that are not. The paired creation-and-revival formula closely matches the commentary's use of fetal creation as evidence for resurrection.

Paul rereads Adam's becoming a living soul against the last Adam as life-giving Spirit. This Christian interpretation directly develops the formed-and-breathed human of Genesis into an eschatological body-and-life contrast.

At the Lord's commanding call, the dead in Christ rise first. It gives a concrete Christian scene of divine sound followed by resurrection, alongside the commentary's recitation and revivification themes.
The psalmist asks to know the measure and extent of his days. This gives a personal, prayerful analogue to the commentary's understanding of qaddara as a life set to a measure.

row.basis: remember Creator in days of youth
row.note: Ecclesiastes calls for remembering the Creator during youth before the difficult days arrive. It makes youth and later decline an ethical frame, matching the commentary's use of completed youth and old age as life stages.

row.basis: spirit and breath made by God
row.note: Isaiah says that the spirit would fail before God, along with the breaths God has made. The verse joins creaturely frailty with divine authorship of breath, though its immediate context is divine restraint from wrath.

Sirach attributes human tongue, eyes, ears, mind, knowledge, and understanding to God. It offers a sapiential expansion of the commentary's properly ordered body into its sensory and cognitive capacities.
Paul says believers will bear the image of the heavenly one. It continues his bodily-resurrection argument by moving from an earthly formed humanity toward a transformed eschatological embodiment.

row.basis: new birth through resurrection to living hope
row.note: First Peter blesses God for giving a new birth into living hope through Jesus' resurrection. It extends the commentary's birth-and-revival nexus into a Christian account of renewed life.

row.basis: earthly tent and enduring divine dwelling
row.note: Paul contrasts the destruction of the earthly tent with an enduring dwelling from God. Its body-as-dwelling image makes the commentary's perishable worldly life and lasting future into an explicit Christian contrast.

row.basis: life as a briefly appearing vapor
row.note: James describes present life as vapor that appears briefly and vanishes. It provides a compact ethical analogue to the commentary's warning that worldly life and its flourishing are transient.
